questions.q: For |+⟩=(|0⟩+|1⟩)/√2, why is P(0)=P(1)=0.5 in the computational basis, while P(+)=1 and P(−)=0 in the X-basis, for the exact same physical state?
options: Because measurement outcomes are basis-relative: |+⟩ is an even split when measured in the computational basis, but is itself exactly the '+' outcome when measured in the X-basis -- both descriptions are correct for their respective basis
Because |+⟩ is secretly two different physical states depending on which basis is used
Because the computational basis result is wrong; only the X-basis result is physically meaningful
Because normalization fails in one of the two bases
questions.explain: The same state gives genuinely different-looking probability distributions depending on measurement basis -- this is not a contradiction, it's the basis-dependence of measurement outcomes covered in Chapter 3.

questions.q: Why does H|+⟩=|0⟩ (exactly, every time) disprove the idea that |+⟩ is just classical 'secretly 0 or secretly 1' uncertainty?
options: A classical probabilistic mixture subjected to any fixed operation would still produce uncertainty afterward, but H reliably reconstructs |0⟩ with certainty -- only possible due to amplitude interference, which plain probability cannot reproduce
Because Hadamard cannot actually be applied to superposition states
Because classical mixtures also reconstruct deterministically under any fixed operation
It doesn't disprove anything; |+⟩ really is just classical uncertainty
questions.explain: Deterministic reconstruction via H·H=I (verified) is only explainable through constructive/destructive interference between amplitudes -- a mechanism with no classical-probability analog.

questions.q: If |ψ⟩=√(1/3)|0⟩+√(2/3)|1⟩ is measured and yields outcome 1, what are the probabilities immediately afterward?
options: P(0)=0 and P(1)=1 with certainty, since the state has collapsed exactly to |1⟩
P(0)=1/3 and P(1)=2/3, unchanged from before the measurement
P(0)=P(1)=0.5, since measurement always resets a qubit to an even split
The probabilities become undefined once a measurement has occurred
questions.explain: The collapse postulate says the state becomes exactly the outcome obtained -- here, |1⟩ -- immediately after measurement, discarding the prior superposition. The original 1/3, 2/3 figures described likelihoods before the measurement happened, not the state afterward.

questions.q: A colleague claims '|0⟩ measured in the X-basis will definitely give +, since |0⟩ is a definite state.' What is wrong with this claim?
options: 'Definite' is basis-relative: |0⟩ is certain only in the computational basis; measured in the X-basis, it gives P(+)=P(−)=0.5, an even split, not a certainty
Nothing is wrong; the claim is entirely correct
The claim is wrong because |0⟩ is not a valid quantum state
The claim is wrong because the X-basis does not actually exist
questions.explain: The colleague is treating 'definite' as an absolute property of the state, when it is really relative to the chosen measurement basis -- |0⟩ is maximally spread out (50/50) when measured in the X-basis, exactly the opposite of certain.

questions.q: For |ψ⟩=0.6|0⟩+0.8|1⟩, if a measurement yields outcome 0 (probability 0.36, verified), what is true about the qubit's state immediately after, and how does this differ from the 36% figure?
options: Immediately after, the qubit is exactly |0⟩ with P(0)=1, P(1)=0 -- the 36% figure described the likelihood of getting this outcome before measurement, not the state that results once it has actually occurred
The qubit remains 0.6|0⟩+0.8|1⟩ unchanged, since measurement doesn't affect superpositions
The qubit becomes an equal superposition, since 36% is close to 50%
The 36% figure describes the post-measurement state directly, with no collapse involved
questions.explain: Collapse means the pre-measurement probability (0.36) only describes the chance of getting outcome 0 -- once that outcome actually occurs, the state updates immediately and completely to |0⟩, with certainty from that point forward, which is a different claim than the prior probability.
